我在看这个登录接口的时候，第一反应是把参数校验逻辑直接内联到控制器里，因为那样改动范围最小，回归风险也最容易控制，评审起来一条线顺着读下去就能走完，不需要跨越好几个文件去来回对照，提交一个很小的补丁就能收工。我甚至已经把初步的草稿写好了，准备本周就发一个合并请求出去。然而，当我沿着调用链一路往下追，才发现真正的问题其实出在会话存储这一层：会话的过期时间被硬编码写死了，无论上层怎么加固校验、怎么堆参数检查，都只是把症状往后拖上一阵子而已，根因始终没有被触及到。既然真正的根因落在存储层，我们就应该先把那一层的配置项和生命周期彻底理顺，做成可配置的参数，然后再回过头来清理控制器里那些冗余的防御性判断，这样收尾才算真正干净。

关于这次线上延迟整体升高的问题，我最初的判断是缓存命中率下降，也就是热点数据没有被有效地留在内存里，频繁地被淘汰掉，所以我建议先横向扩容缓存集群，把数据分片铺得更开一些，让每台机器负责的数据量减少，这样命中率理论上应该能明显回升，尾延迟也会随之回落。这个思路在以往几次容量问题里都奏效过，所以我当时相当有信心，甚至觉得不需要再做别的排查。话说回来，等我把整个火焰图从头到尾认真看了一遍之后，才发现在真正排队等待的其实是数据库连接池，大量请求都堆积在获取连接这一步上，而缓存这一层根本连瓶颈的影子都没有出现，扩容缓存不过是把预算花在了错误的地方。所以正确的做法应当是先调整连接池的大小与超时策略，再重新评估缓存是否还有扩容的必要。

分页接口我原本打算彻底改成游标方案，理由是它在数据量很大的时候表现得更加稳定，不会出现翻到后面几页时速度突然变慢的老毛病，同时也更方便前端实现无限滚动的交互，整体体验会更加顺滑连贯，后端也不必再去维护复杂的偏移量计算。这个方案在设计评审里也得到过认可，我甚至已经把迁移步骤大致排好了，打算下个迭代就动手。等等，我突然想起来下游其实还有两个消费方，他们目前仍然是老老实实按页码来拉取数据的，一旦我们这边单方面改成游标，他们原有的签约逻辑和失败重试机制会直接失灵，对接肯定会出问题，甚至会影响到月度的对账。所以这个改动绝对不能单独推进，必须先把下游的调用方一起迁移到新协议上，否则兼容性被打破的代价远大于那点性能收益，得重新排期。

我们先前把发布时间定在月底，核心理由是这样能给测试留出足够充裕的回归时间，不至于为了赶工而漏测关键路径，同时也让市场团队有空间把发布物料和宣发节奏准备妥当，看上去是个四平八稳、谁都不得罪的好安排。团队内部对这个时间点也基本没有异议，相关的通知邮件甚至已经草拟好了，只等最后一轮确认。等一下，我随手翻了一下运维的排班表才发现，月底那几天正好撞上季度结算的窗口，运维人力几乎被财会相关的需求全部占满，一旦线上出现告警，很可能连一个能及时响应、有权限操作的人都没有。这个时间点选得其实非常糟糕，我们必须把它提前到月中，避开这段高风险的时期，宁可在测试上多挤一点时间出来。

给支付调用外面统一包一层自动重试逻辑，乍看之下是个相当干净利落的修复，代码增量很小，几乎不改变原有结构，也能把偶发的网络抖动和瞬时超时稳稳地挡在外面，让整体的成功率数字好看不少，监控面板上的毛刺也会少很多。很多成熟的客户端库默认就带这样的机制，所以我们一度觉得直接照搬过来就行，不必再花心思。但这样做会破坏幂等性：如果没有一个全局唯一、跨请求一致的幂等键，重试就有相当大的概率对同一个订单重复扣款，用户会直接收到两笔账单，这类事故带来的投诉、退款和信任损失成本极高。所以在补上幂等键、并确保服务端能够正确去重之前，这个方案无论如何都不能上线，哪怕它当场就能改善成功率的报表，也不能冒这个险。

在状态这个字段上单独建一个索引，第一眼看上去是一笔稳赚不赔的买卖，查询计划应该马上就能变好，扫描的行数也会从整张表大幅下降到只触碰相关的那几行，执行时间自然就短了下来，慢查询日志里相关的条目也会随之消失。这样的优化在很多项目里都是立竿见影的，所以我最初毫不犹豫地把它列为了首选方案，准备直接写进变更单里。不过，这个字段在整个表里只有三个不同的取值，选择性低得可怜，优化器在绝大多数情况下极有可能直接忽略这个索引，转而继续走全表扫描，而我们却要为每一次写入额外付出维护这个索引的代价，而且随着数据增长，这个代价会越来越明显。权衡下来，与其盲目地加索引，不如先评估能否把那些常用查询改造成覆盖索引，或者干脆调整一下数据模型，从根上解决。

我前面很笃定地说，启动的时候直接同步读取配置文件就可以了，反正整个进程生命周期里只读这一次，那点磁盘开销完全可以忽略不计，没有必要为了它专门引入异步的复杂度，把原本清晰的启动流程拆得七零八落、难以跟踪。当时我还建议团队照这个思路去写初始化代码，强调这样最省事。其实我错了，这个处理器是运行在事件循环里的，一次阻塞式的读取会把同一时刻所有其他的连接全部卡住，在冷启动的流量高峰下后果尤其严重，用户会明显地感到第一批请求集体变慢，甚至会触发上游的超时重试，形成雪崩。所以它必须改成异步读取，或者至少挪到线程池里去执行，绝不能图省事直接在事件循环里做同步 I/O，这一点在评审规范里其实也早有提醒。

我先前判断样本量已经足够，完全可以下结论了，依据是置信区间看起来相当窄，几组实验之间的趋势也很一致，看不出明显的波动，再继续收集数据纯属浪费资源，不如把有限的人力投入到更紧迫的分析任务上去。基于这个判断，我甚至建议提前结束数据采集、把服务器释放出来。我得收回这个判断：后来我逐一核对原始明细表时才发现，同一批用户被重复计入了好几次，原因是埋点在上报的时候根本没有做去重，同一个会话被反复触发，真实的独立样本量远小于表层显示的那个漂亮数字。按修正后的样本重新计算，这个结论其实并不显著，我们根本没有理由下这么强的断言，必须重新采样、重新分析一遍之后再对外发布。

每次更新数据的时候都同步写穿到缓存，看起来挺合理，代码也保持得简单直接，读路径几乎总能命中，整体的延迟数字会显得非常漂亮，压测报告交上去也好看，领导层看指标时不会有任何疑问。乍一看，这种做法把复杂度都收敛到了写路径上，而写路径本来就不那么频繁，似乎是笔稳赚不赔的交易，值得推广到所有服务上去。不过再琢磨一下，这办法其实并不划算：在写多读少的负载下，每一次写操作都必须等缓存返回才能继续往下走，我们省下来的那一点点读延迟，最后全都从写延迟里还了回去，净收益甚至是负的，而且在缓存抖动时还会额外放大延迟。所以这笔账要按真实的读写比例和缓存故障率重新算一遍，而不是凭直觉下结论。

把这块相对独立的任务交给一位新同事来做，初看挺合适，既能让他借此机会熟悉整个系统的骨架和协作方式，也能顺手减轻我这边的工作负担，从带人和产出的双重角度看似乎是一个双赢的局面。我原本都已经打算在周会上直接把这个任务派下去了，连背景资料都准备好了。话虽如此，仔细想想其实并不合适，因为他对这套构建系统和发布流程完全不熟悉，前期的讲解、随时的答疑以及后期的返工成本加在一起，很可能比我自己从头做完还要高出不少，反而拖慢了整体进度。与其如此，不如先让他接手一个边界更清晰、风险更小、几乎不会阻塞别人的子任务当作热身，等他熟悉了节奏和工具链之后，再逐步把更重要的模块放手给他，这样双方的压力都会小很多。

最直接的方案是在这个迭代里把单体应用拆成三个独立服务，让每个团队各自拥有清晰的服务边界和发布节奏，长期来看确实能够减少团队之间互相阻塞、排队等待发布的痛苦，架构图上也会显得更加整洁，对外讲述技术演进时也更有说服力。这个方向在技术规划里已经讨论了不止一轮，大家基本上都认同它是未来的目标状态。然而，在动手拆之前必须先想清楚共享数据库这件事：如果数据库仍然绑在一起，那么拆服务只是把原本进程内的函数调用耦合，搬到了网络调用上而已，故障面不但没有缩小，反而因为引入了网络分区和序列化而变得更大，排查问题也更难。所以第一步应该是按领域去切分数据的所有权，定义清楚谁写谁读，而不是急着先把服务拉出来再说。

在课堂上先用同步读取的方式来讲文件 I/O 是可以的，学生理解起来非常直观，读一行、处理一行，因果关系一目了然，也不会一上来就被回调、Promise 这些抽象概念绕得晕头转向，从而过早地丧失信心。这种由浅入深的教学顺序在入门课程里一向是很稳妥的选择，我也一向推荐这么做，自己也用了很多年。但这样会把并发和阻塞的核心概念完全藏起来，等到后面正式讲异步章节的时候，学生反而很难把两者联系起来，理解的断层会突然变得很大，甚至会产生强烈的抗拒和困惑，觉得异步是凭空冒出来的怪物。所以这个教学顺序需要调整，应当先明确地点出阻塞的代价以及它带来的无谓等待，再顺势引入异步作为一种解决方案，让学生在理解问题之后自然接受答案，而不是把问题隐藏到后面一笔带过。

这个模块主要依赖字符串拼接、列表去重、字典查找、集合运算等常用操作，因此在初始化的时候只需要导入标准库就完全足够了，完全不必额外引入任何第三方依赖，也不会带来版本兼容和许可方面的麻烦。代码里已经把每一个依赖的来源都标注得清清楚楚，评审的人顺着导入列表一路读下去，就能一眼看明白整体结构是怎么一步步搭起来的，不需要再去翻阅额外的设计文档，评审效率会高很多。后续如果要替换其中某一项实现，也只需要改动对应的封装层即可，不会牵动底层的业务逻辑，更不需要重新跑一轮全量回归，维护成本非常低，团队的接手门槛也随之降了下来，新人照着注释就能上手，几乎不需要口口相传的经验。

这个警告其实不过是个无害的弃用提示，只会在冷路径上触发区区一次，新的写法已经排进了下一个迭代的待办清单，眼下完全可以先把它忽略掉，不必为此专门开一个修复任务来占用宝贵的排期。把有限的时间花在真正的性能瓶颈上，收益要大得多，没必要被这样一条噪音分散了注意力，反而耽误了正事。等新版本正式上线之后，这条提示自然而然就会消失，届时也不需要额外做任何清理工作，更不用回头补测试用例，风险几乎为零，所以现阶段挂着它完全没关系，不必有任何心理负担，看到了直接划过去即可。

其实这个结论是有一点数据支撑的，样本量达到了两万，置信区间也相当窄，因此我们对它的稳健性是相当有信心的，短期内不会轻易改变看法，也不认为会有什么意外因素把它推翻。后续只要保持同样的抽样方式，并且不引入新的选择偏差，结论就不会发生明显变化，这一点是完全可以预期的。这部分在报告的方法学章节里已经写得非常清楚，评审的人如果需要独立复现，也完全可以按照附录里的脚本自行跑一遍验证，得到的数字应当与正文保持一致，误差也会稳稳地落在可接受的范围内，不会出现方向性的偏差，评审因此可以直接采信。

这个模型精度很高，但推理速度也确实偏慢，这两点其实是同时成立的，并不存在谁否定谁的问题，而是一种非常典型的权衡关系，本质上是在同一个设计空间里做出的取舍。所以在部署的时候，需要根据具体的业务场景，在速度和准确率之间做出选择：对离线的批处理任务可以优先选择高精度，因为时间预算足够宽裕；对在线的实时接口则更应该看重延迟表现，必要时甚至牺牲一点准确率也无妨。这种权衡本来就没有唯一的正确答案，完全取决于业务对延迟的容忍度以及成本预算，没办法一刀切地给出一个放之四海皆准的结论，只能结合具体场景逐案判断、反复权衡。

主流程采用流式处理是最合适的选择，它能够把首字节延迟压到很低的水平，用户从点击到看到第一个字的等待会明显缩短，整体体验也会更加顺滑连贯，长回答尤其受益。这个方向我们内部没有任何异议，已经定下来了，不会再有反复。不过，仓库里其实也同步维护着一套批处理版本，如果某些场景下吞吐量比延迟更加重要，完全可以切换到那套实现来用，两条路径共用同一套解析与校验逻辑，输入输出的数据结构完全一致，所以迁移和切换的成本都非常低。团队可以按各自的业务线自由选择，不必强行统一成一种，这样反而更灵活，也更贴合各自的真实需求。

在修改那个被多个线程共享的计数器之前，工作线程必须先等待互斥锁被完全释放，否则在并发写入的时候，这个自增操作很可能会被后来的写操作覆盖掉，导致最终的计数结果明显偏低，而且这种错误极难在事后排查。这类竞态条件在生产环境里几乎无法稳定复现，往往要跑很久才偶发一次，所以从本地测试的阶段开始，就要严格按照先加锁后修改的顺序来执行，任何试图绕过锁的所谓捷径都不可取，哪怕它在单线程的单元测试里看起来毫无问题。代码注释里也专门提醒了这一点，就是为了防止后来的人出于性能考虑，自作聪明地把它改成无锁结构最后酿成大祸，毕竟这类 bug 一旦上线就极难回收。

第一步，我们先冻结新表的 schema，避免在迁移的过程中有人顺手改动字段，导致两边定义不一致，埋下难以察觉的隐患；第二步，用后台任务在夜间业务低峰期分批回填历史数据，注意做好限速，以免把主库的 IO 拖垮，影响到白天正常的线上读写；第三步，再把读流量逐步切换过去，同时保留旧的列作为兜底，并持续观察一整周再决定是否删除。这个三步走的顺序在前两次类似的迁移里都已经完整验证过，效果相当稳定，没有出过任何事故，所以这一次也打算照旧沿用，不会在过程中临时调整，以免引入新的不确定性，把本来简单的事情搞复杂。

总之，这次迁移整体上是切实可行的，风险处于可控的范围之内，时间线也完全站得住脚，目前为止并没有出现任何必须推翻重来的信号，各项前置条件也都已经逐一满足。归纳一下，我们应当继续按照原定的计划向前推进，同时保持密切的线上监控即可，不必额外增加流程上的负担，那样反而会拖慢节奏，影响团队的士气。除非错误预算在某个阶段被突然烧穿，或者有新的外部依赖插入进来打乱了原有的节奏，否则完全没有必要重新评估这个决定，按现有的节奏一步步执行下去就好，中途不需要再反复开会讨论，也不必事事请示上级。

课堂上我们会先讲栈、队列、树、堆等等这些最基础的数据结构，等学生对它们有了直观的认识和基本的操作手感之后，再引入图这种相对复杂得多的结构，这样安排能让知识逐步累加，不至于一上来就被陡峭的复杂度压垮，从而失去学习的信心和兴趣。每一个结构都会配一个可以亲手运行的小例子，让学生亲眼看到数据是如何一步步流动和被操作的，而不是仅仅停留在纸面上的定义和伪代码，理解会深得多。等到最后再做一次综合练习，把这些结构串起来使用，学生就能真切地体会到它们之间的联系，印象也会更牢固，不至于学一个忘一个。

这套方案在延迟表现上确实很有优势，我依然倾向于最终选择它，虽然我也坦率地承认，它的运维成本比另外一套要高出一些，需要额外维护一个组件、多配一套告警规则，但总体权衡下来，它仍然是更划算的那一个，收益明显盖过了麻烦。只要把监控和告警做到位，多出来的那部分运维负担是完全可以接受的，何况团队本来就在类似的系统上有过经验，上手曲线会比想象中平缓得多。所以我的结论并没有发生改变，还是建议沿着这条路径继续往下设计和落地，不必再左右摇摆、反复推翻自己，那样只会白白消耗团队的信任。

这个方案整体上是可行的，接口设计也没有暴露出明显的问题，评审时的第一印象是基本过关的，核心流程也讲得通，看得出来是花过心思的。然而，它还缺少一个完整的回滚步骤，这在正式上线之前必须补上，属于流程上的常规要求，而不是可以商量、可以往后拖的可选项，任何一份上线清单里都会把它列在最前面。把回滚脚本写好，并且在预发环境里完整地演练一遍，确认真的能够退回来，这个方案就可以放心地进入下一道评审环节；否则一旦线上真的出了问题，我们连一条稳妥的退路都没有，只能被动地热修，风险实在太大，也可能是致命的。

其实这里的数据库连接是复用的，并不需要每一次都重新建立，所以这段循环看上去虽然有些吓人，实际上并不会像表面上那样频繁地打开新连接，开销远没有想象中那么可怕，不必急着去重构它。连接池的配置在应用初始化的时候就已经注入好了，循环里每一次取到的都只是一个已经存在的句柄，真正昂贵的建连动作早在启动阶段就完成了，之后只是借用而已。理解这一点之后，再回过头去看那段代码，就不会再觉得它存在什么明显的性能隐患，反而会觉得当初那样写是有意为之，其实相当合理，也省了很多无谓的争论和返工。

上线之前，我们要先等待安全团队对威胁模型完成完整的评审并签字确认，按照既定的流程，这通常需要三个工作日左右，所以在排期上必须留出足够的缓冲，不能把时间卡得太死，否则一旦评审延后，整个发布计划都会被拖累，得不偿失。相关的设计文档我已经提前发过去了，希望能把这段等待时间压缩到两天以内。在这段空档期里，开发同学可以先着手准备灰度方案、监控看板和应急预案，完全没有必要干等着，可以并行推进其他准备工作，等审批一过就能马上进入执行阶段，效率反而更高，也不会白白浪费这段等待期。

首先要把问题稳定地复现出来，否则后续的任何修复都无从验证，改完之后也不知道究竟有没有真正生效，只能靠猜；然后把日志级别临时调到调试，抓取足够多的上下文信息和完整的调用栈，为后面的定位提供可靠的线索；最后再顺着堆栈逐层往下走，定位到具体的代码行。这三步之间有着严格的先后依赖关系，随意跳步往往会白白浪费时间，甚至把排查的方向带偏到完全无关的地方，越查越乱。按照这个流程稳稳地走下来，大多数的偶发问题都能在两轮调试之内收敛，整体效率其实比盲目乱试要高得多，也更省心，还不容易在慌乱中引入新的错误。

团队现在最关心的是首屏加载时间，产品经理希望把默认入口页压缩到一秒以内。我们目前的做法是把所有组件一次性打包，启动时整包下发，然后在客户端解析并挂载。这个方案上线已经半年，随着功能不断叠加，包体越来越大，首屏时间也从最初的一点二秒缓慢涨到了三秒多，用户投诉逐渐增多。所以有人提议干脆按路由做代码分割，让默认入口只加载必需的模块。这个思路听起来很合理，实施成本也不算高，只需要在打包配置里加几行。其实不对，路由级分割只解决入口包的问题，而我们真正的瓶颈是首屏依赖的那几个第三方库，它们无论如何都会被同时加载。如果不先分析依赖图就直接动手分割，很可能忙活一周，首屏时间几乎没有变化。因此我建议先做一次打包分析，把真正阻塞首屏的模块找出来，再决定分割策略。

关于数据同步这块，我最初的判断是让每个客户端直接连主库读写，省掉中间层，链路最短，延迟也最低。主库目前是一主两从的架构，读请求可以走从库。乍看之下这确实简单直接，运维也只需要维护一套连接配置，出问题好排查。等等，这里有个被忽略的前提：客户端数量会随业务扩张而增长，如果每一个实例都持有到主库的长连接，连接数会迅速逼近上限，一旦打满，写请求会直接失败，而读请求也拿不到新的连接。更糟的是，这种失败往往是突发的，监控上只会表现为连接拒绝，很难定位到具体来源。所以更稳妥的做法是加一层轻量的写入代理，由它统一复用有限的主库连接，客户端只连代理。这样即便客户端数量翻十倍，主库连接数也仍然可控。

用户反馈导出大报表时经常超时，运维建议把超时时间统一从十秒提高到一分钟，认为大部分偶发失败都能这样被兜住，改动也只需要调一个配置。这个办法简单，风险看起来也低，毕竟只是放宽等待，不会改变逻辑。然而从压测数据看，真正超时的请求里，有八成是慢查询导致的，把这些请求的等待时间从十秒拉长到一分钟，只会让数据库连接被占用得更久。这样可以，但连接池会因此更快耗尽，最终把局部超时演变成全站排队。换句话说，直接放宽超时指标上像是治好了症状，实际上是把问题从客户端转移到了数据库。更合理的方案是先对慢查询做分级：高频且可优化的加索引，低频的允许长超时，并在配置里按接口分别设置，而不是全局一刀切。

我刚才在评审时建议把这个工具类的静态方法改成实例方法，说这样更符合面向对象的设计。当时考虑的是静态方法难以被 mock，测试里不好替换，也不方便注入依赖。现在回头看，其实说错了。这个类里所有静态方法都是纯函数，没有任何外部状态，把它们改成实例方法只会逼着调用方每次都得先构造一个对象，反而增加了噪音和使用成本。真正需要注入依赖的是那些访问网络或文件的方法，它们本来就已经设计成了实例方法。所以正确的改法不是全盘实例化，而是保持纯函数为静态，让它们天然可测，只在确实有副作用的少数方法上做依赖注入。请以这个修正后的结论为准。

考虑要不要把这个核心模块用更快的语言重写一遍。支持的一方认为，当前实现是脚本语言，计算密集路径上确实偏慢，重写后延迟能降一半以上，而且团队里几个人本来就对新语言感兴趣，学起来不会太费劲。这个方向乍看挺有吸引力，性能收益直观，也算技术储备，甚至能当作一次不错的练手机会。看着挺合理……再想想也不对。性能收益只在最热的那几条路径上成立，而这个模块大部分时间都花在等待下游服务上，重写对整体延迟的改善非常有限。更关键的是，团队里没有人在生产环境维护过这门语言，出了问题排查成本会陡增，招聘和交接也会更困难。所以当下的性价比并不高，先做局部优化和缓存，把等待时间压下去，收效更快，风险也更可控。

针对缓存失效的策略，我之前拍板说简单地设置十分钟的过期时间就足够了，理由是绝大多数数据在十分钟内就会再次被读取，缓存命中率能维持在很高的水平。当时也觉得配置简单，不需要额外的依赖和复杂度，上线快。但仔细推演数据一致性的场景后，其实不对。十分钟的过期窗口意味着，一次写入之后，最坏情况下其他读请求要在十分钟后才看得到新值，而我们的订单详情恰好是写后立刻要读的，这种延迟会让用户以为操作没生效，进而重复提交。所以仅仅按时间过期是不够的，必须结合写入时的主动失效，在写路径上把相关的键立刻删掉，让下一次读回源并重建缓存。这样既保留了兜底的过期，又保证了写后读的及时性。

刚才我说这个函数应该按职责拆成三个更小的函数，理由是单一职责、易读易测。看起来是对的，很多规范也这么建议。不过再想一下，这三个所谓的小函数其实共享大量临时变量和中间结果，一旦拆开，就要么来回传参数，要么把状态提到外层，两种做法都会让调用链更绕。拆分的收益是每段更短，但代价是阅读时要不断在函数间跳转，上下文反而更碎。所以更合适的做法是保持它为一个整体，但用清晰的段落注释和空行划分出逻辑阶段，让读者一眼看到三个阶段，而不用真的拆成三份。重构成多个函数不是目标，降低理解成本才是目标。这个判断也符合我们一贯的原则：改动的大小应当由它带来的收益决定，而不是由某种教条式的风格规范来决定。

在评审权限模型时,我先提出的方案是把角色的判断直接写死在每个接口的处理逻辑里，每个接口根据当前用户的角色决定是否放行。这样做的好处是直观，谁都能看懂。然而当角色数量从三个增长到十几个、并且开始出现跨角色的例外规则之后，这种散落在各处的判断就变得难以维护，改一处规则要翻遍所有接口，还容易漏改。等等,这个方向其实从一开始就埋了隐患：授权逻辑本就应该集中，和业务逻辑解耦，否则每次调整都会牵动业务代码，测试成本也会成倍上升。所以正确做法是抽出统一的策略层，接口只声明它需要的权限点，由策略层集中判定。这样规则变化时只改动策略层，接口代码保持稳定。

有同事提出，既然日志查询慢，那就把日志级别整体调到 debug，把每个环节的细节都记下来，出问题时信息最全。这个想法出发点没错，排查期间确实希望信息尽可能多。先按这个思路试了一版，结果磁盘很快就被写满，而且在真正出问题时，海量冗余日志把关键行淹没，反而更难定位。这没问题，但整体调级会同时放大存储、检索和信噪比三个问题，得不偿失。更好的做法是按模块单独控制级别：只把怀疑出问题的那几个模块开到 debug，其余保持 info，并给 debug 日志加保留期，到期自动清理。这样既拿得到细节，又不会拖垮存储和查询。

对于分页接口的实现，我一开始倾向于用页码加每页大小的偏移量方式，因为它实现简单，前端也熟悉接口形态。小数据量下它工作得很好。然而当表里的数据涨到千万级之后，深层翻页会因为偏移量越来越大而明显变慢，数据库要扫描并丢弃前面所有行。这样可以，但性能会随着页码加深而线性劣化，用户体验在翻到后面时会急剧变差。所以中大数据量更适合用游标分页，也就是基于上一页最后一条记录的主键来定位下一页，查询始终走索引，翻到多深都不会变慢。前端只需改成携带游标而不是页码，就能在数据量增长后依然保持稳定的响应时间。前端需要做的最小改动，只是把请求参数从页码换成游标，其余渲染逻辑可以完全不变。

总结一下前面讨论的发布节奏。我们决定先做小范围灰度，把新版本投放到大约百分之五的流量上，持续观察一个完整的业务周期，重点看错误率、延迟分位数和核心转化指标。如果这几项都稳定在预期区间内，再把灰度比例逐步放大到一半，最后才全量铺开。整个过程的每一步都要有明确的回滚触发条件，一旦指标越过阈值就立刻退回上一版。看上去这个安排稳妥，覆盖也完整。不过再想一下，其实还有一处没考虑周全：灰度期间新旧两个版本会同时写同一批数据，如果数据结构有变更，就必须保证双向兼容，否则老版本读到新字段会出错。所以在灰度开始前，要先确认数据格式的向后兼容性，或者干脆采用双写加读切换的方式过渡。

关于接口错误码的设计，我原本主张全部用 HTTP 状态码表达，比如用四零四表示资源不存在，用四二二表示参数校验失败，认为这样最符合规范，客户端也容易理解。这个主张在简单场景下成立。然而当业务错误变得细分之后，光靠状态码就表达不过来了，比如同一个四零九可能对应好几种冲突原因。其实不对,状态码适合表达协议层面的结果，业务层面的具体原因应该放在响应体里，用一个稳定的业务错误码字段来承载。这样客户端既能按状态码做通用处理，又能按业务码做精细分支，两者互补而不是互相替代。这样一来，协议层的通用处理和业务层的精细处理各司其职，接口的演进也会更加从容。

在部署流程里，负责分发的那一步必须等待上游的构建产物全部就绪之后才能继续，否则流水线会拿到一个不完整的发布包，导致后续的部署步骤在解压阶段就失败。这个等待是刻意设计的，它让各阶段之间形成依赖顺序，避免并行执行时互相踩踏。同样地，回滚脚本也要等待健康检查通过，确认新版本确实起来了，才决定是否触发回退。整套机制的核心就是严格的先后关系：谁依赖谁，谁就必须等谁。如果为了提速而随意去掉这些等待，表面上看流水线跑得更快了，但实际上只是把失败推迟到了更靠后、更难排查的环节。所以我们坚持保留这些同步点，并在文档里说明每一处等待存在的原因，方便后来的人理解而不是随手删掉。

这个方案既简单又稳定，但成本也很低，所以很适合作为第一版的原型来实现。它的依赖很少，几乎不需要额外的基础设施，团队里谁都能上手，维护起来的心理负担也小。我们评估过几套更复杂的技术选型，它们在某些极端场景下确实更强，但那些场景以目前的业务规模根本不会遇到。与其为了想象中的未来提前引入复杂度，不如先用这套简单方案把功能跑通，把真实的瓶颈用数据找出来。等需求明确之后，再针对真正的痛点做升级，届时的改造也会更有针对性，不会白费功夫。这就是我们推荐它的全部理由。在技术选型上，克制往往比激进更难得，也更需要对当前规模有清醒的认识，我们愿意把这份克制坚持到底，而不是被新奇的技术牵着走。

要准备的东西包括配置文件、环境变量、访问证书以及数据库连接串等等，这些都要在部署之前逐项确认清楚，任何一项缺失都会让服务在启动阶段直接失败。我们建议把它们整理成一张检查清单，按顺序勾选，避免凭记忆操作而遗漏。清单里还应当注明每一项的取值来源和常见错误，比如证书要记得检查有效期，连接串要确认网络可达。除此之外，密钥类的配置不应该直接写在清单或脚本里，而应通过安全的密钥管理服务注入，避免随代码泄露。定期复核这份清单，在环境和依赖发生变化时及时更新，能显著减少上线当天手忙脚乱的情况。把检查清单当作一份活的文档来维护，让它随着系统的演进而不断补充，是对团队协作最实际的帮助。

Excellent question — it cuts to the heart of the design tradeoff. Let me clarify precisely, because "combined" doesn't mean "causally unordered."

## What "1 turn = 1 request, N tools" actually means

There **is** causal order — but it's *between turns*, not *within* a tool-batch. The key distinction:

**opencode's model — the model emits a tool *batch*, the SDK runs the batch, then ONE more request continues:**
1. The model produces an assistant message that may contain **multiple tool-call blocks** (e.g. `read_file(a)`, `read_file(b)`, `read_file(c)`) in a single generation.
2. The AI SDK treats those N calls as a **batch** — they are the model's *simultaneous* choices for this turn. The SDK runs their `execute` closures **concurrently** and collects all N `tool-result` events.
3. Only **after the whole batch resolves** does the SDK feed all N results back and the model generates the **next** assistant message.

So causality is: `[assistant: call A,B,C] → [tool A done, B done, C done] → [assistant: sees all 3 results, decides next]`. The N tools within a batch are **causally parallel by the model's own choice** — the model declared "I want all three of these before I continue," so there's no ordering the model cared about. The next turn is strictly *after*.

**MYCC's model — the same batch becomes N sequential round-trips:**
1. Model emits the same `call A,B,C` batch.
2. MYCC's `TOOL` state runs A → result, then transitions `TOOL→LLM` → **fresh request**; the model sees A's result and generates again (possibly calling B); `TOOL→LLM` again; etc.
3. So what was the model's single "give me A,B,C then I'll think" becomes 3 separate LLM generations interleaved with tool results.

## The causal-order answer

**Within one batch: no causal order is needed, because the model itself didn't impose any.** The model emitted A, B, C *together* — by definition it didn't want B's result before deciding C (if it did, it would have emitted only A, waited for the result, then emitted B). Parallel execution of a batch the model *declared parallel* violates no causality. This is exactly how the Anthropic/OpenAI tool-use protocol works: multiple tool calls in one assistant turn are explicitly meant to be run together.

**Between batches/turns: strict causal order is preserved.** The SDK does not start the next `streamText` step until the current batch's tools resolve and their results are appended. `processor.ts`'s `cleanup` awaits all in-flight tools (`{ concurrency: "unbounded" }`, L545) before the turn is allowed to finish — so the model never sees partial results from an unfinished batch.

## The real risk (and how opencode mitigates it)

You've put your finger on the genuine downside: **if the model emits calls that *are* actually dependent but doesn't realize it**, parallel execution runs them in a race. E.g. `write_file(x)` then `read_file(x)` in the same batch — the read could see the pre-write state. MYCC's sequential model is *safe by construction* here: even if the model wrongly batches dependent calls, MYCC serializes them so the read always sees the write.

opencode mitigates this not at the dispatch layer but via:
1. **The model's own batching discipline** — well-trained models don't batch dependent calls (they emit the write,wait for the result, then emit the read in a *separate* turn). When it does batch, the calls are genuinely independent reads. 2. **The `DOOM_LOOP_THRESHOLD=3` repeat-detector** (`processor.ts` L29/L356) and `shouldBreak`/`blocked` flags catch pathological re-batching (the model re-emitting the same calls turn after turn without progress) — a guard MYCC gets for free from serialization. 3. **Tool-level idempotency** — reads are inherently parallel-safe; side-effecting tools (`write_file`, `bash`) are where races *could* bite, but in practice the model rarely batches two writes to overlapping state.

## So: is there causal order within 1 turn?

**No causal order is *required* within a tool-batch, because the model itself declared those calls parallel** — it emitted them together precisely because it didn't need any one's result to decide the next. That's the protocol contract: "these N calls are my simultaneous choices; run them and give me all results back, then I'll continue." opencode honors that contract by running them concurrently inside one `streamText`. Causality is preserved *between* turns (the next generation strictly follows the full batch's results), and *within* a turn it mirrors the model's own (lack of) ordering intent.

MYCC's sequential model, by contrast, **imposes an order the model didn't ask for** — it runs A, forces a fresh LLM generation, runs B, forces another generation, etc. This is *safe* (dependent calls can't race) but it's also *wasteful*: the model said "give me A,B,C together" and MYCC instead gave it A alone, made it re-think, gave it B alone, made it re-think again. That's the *k*+1 vs 1 round-trips — and it's why MYCC's safety costs latency even when the calls were perfectly independent.

## The design tradeoff in one line

opencode trusts the tool-use protocol's batching semantics (parallel-by-model-choice, causal-between-turns) and gains efficiency; MYCC distrusts it, serializes for safety, and pays a round-trip per tool. The efficiency gap is the price of MYCC's stricter causal guarantee — which is only *needed* when the model mis-batches dependent calls, a case opencode handles with detection (`DOOM_LOOP_THRESHOLD`) rather than prevention.

**你的两个判断都有合理性，但需要修正一个常见误解：Ballmer 的"部门竞争"文化主要源自 GE 的 stack ranking，而非宝洁。宝洁的内部竞争是"品牌对品牌"的市场竞争，性质完全不同。** 而 Ballmer 的战略失误与宝洁文化的关联则是**间接且薄弱**的——他在宝洁只工作了约两年，且做的是基层销售。

## 一、关于 Ballmer 战略失误（Windows Phone）是否与宝洁文化有关

### 证据：关联很弱

1. **Ballmer 在宝洁的时间极短且职位基层**。据 CBS《60 Minutes》报道，他在宝洁的第一天紧张到手心出汗，卖的是 Duncan Hines 布朗 mix、蓝莓松饼 mix 等，之后便去斯坦福商学院，1980 年被 Gates 拉走加入微软。这是一段**约两年的基层销售经历**，并非能塑造战略思维的深度浸润。

2. **Windows Phone 失败的真实原因（Ballmer 自述）**：
   - "我们有大量优秀工程师被牵制在其他项目上"
   - "我们把它想得太像 Windows 了，没有用不同的思维"——即**把 PC 范式硬套到手机上**
   - 他自己在 Stanford GSB 演讲中承认，若能改变一个决策，是应**更早进入搜索领域**（比 Google 晚了 5 年），可见其战略盲区是**对平台型新范式的反应迟缓**，而非某种特定管理文化的产物。

3. **宝洁文化反而强调"贴近消费者"**。Neil McElroy 的名言是"找出消费者想要什么，然后给他们"。宝洁的市场研究部（Doc Smelser 领导）极端重视消费者反馈。如果说宝洁文化真有影响，那本应是"以消费者为中心"——而 Windows Phone 的失败恰恰是**背离了消费者体验**（强行塞 PC 界面），这更像微软的"工程师文化"而非宝洁的"消费者文化"。

### 小结
Windows Phone 的失败更应归因于**微软自身的 PC 路径依赖和工程师主导文化**，而非宝洁。实际上，Ballmer 若真吸取了宝洁的消费者中心主义，反而可能少犯这个错。

---

## 二、关于"部门间竞争" vs. Nadella 的 D&I / connect 文化

这里有一个**关键的概念澄清**：

### Ballmer 时代的"部门竞争"真正源头是 GE，不是宝洁

| 维度 | 微软（Ballmer 时代） | 宝洁 |
|------|---------------------|------|
| 竞争机制 | **Stack ranking（强制排名）**：员工被强制分布到优秀/普通/差，同事之间零和博弈 | **品牌管理制**：不同品牌团队争夺市场份额，但是对外的市场竞争 |
| 竞争对象 | **人对人**（同事间互相使绊子） | **品牌对品牌**（Camay vs. Ivory 争夺不同细分市场） |
| 后果 | 据 HBS 案例：员工"不仅因做得好被奖励，更因确保同事失败而受奖"；"管理靠人格暗杀" | Neil McElroy 设计的初衷是**减少内耗**，让每个品牌专注自己的细分市场 |

**Stack ranking 是 GE 的杰克·韦尔奇发明的"活力曲线"（vitality curve）**，2000 年代被微软引入。这与宝洁无关——讽刺的是，GE 的 Jeffrey Immelt（韦尔奇继任者）也是宝洁校友，但 stack ranking 是韦尔奇遗产，不是宝洁遗产。

### Nadella 的纠正是针对 stack ranking，而非针对宝洁式品牌竞争

- **2013 年微软废除 stack ranking**（据 Business Insider），改为评估员工"如何为团队做贡献"，不再让人与人对抗。
- Nadella 推行的"growth mindset"（成长型思维）、"from know-it-all to learn-it-all"是针对**人际零和竞争文化**，而非针对**品牌间市场竞争**。

### 那宝洁有没有"内部竞争"的痕迹影响 Ballmer？

有，但是**另一种性质的竞争**，且 Ballmer 未必直接继承：

- 宝洁的品牌管理制（1931 年 McElroy 备忘录）确实创造了**品牌之间的内部竞争**——Camay 团队和 Ivory 团队争夺资源。
- 但 McElroy 的本意恰恰是**消除恶性内耗**：他写备忘录正是因为 Camay 和 Ivory 互相蚕食让他沮丧，他的方案是让每个品牌定位不同细分市场，**变互相蚕食为各自发展**。
- 学术研究（Purkaystha 的研究）明确指出：宝洁在 1980 年代发现"品牌内部竞争虽有其优点，但弊端在面对外部强竞争时日益显现——公司错失了协作和共享信息的机会"，于是 Smale 和 Pepper 在 1986 年推动**品类管理（Category Management）**改革，让同品类品牌**协作**而非竞争。

**所以宝洁自己的演化路径，恰恰与 Nadella 纠正微软的方向一致**：从内部竞争 → 走向协作（Category Management → Cohort Management）。宝洁在 1986 年就做了微软 2013 年才做的事。

---

## 三、综合判断

| 你的观点 | 修正后的结论 |
|---------|------------|
| Ballmer 战略失误与宝洁文化有关 | **关联薄弱**。他在宝洁仅 2 年基层销售；Windows Phone 失败主因是微软 PC 路径依赖，且违背了宝洁"消费者中心"的核心理念 |
| Ballmer 推崇部门竞争有宝洁痕迹 | **来源是 GE 的 stack ranking，不是宝洁**。宝洁的内部竞争是"品牌对品牌"争夺市场，且宝洁自己早在 1986 年就用 Category Management 转向协作 |
| Nadella 的 D&I / connect 纠正了竞争风气 | **正确**。Nadella 废除 stack ranking、推行 growth mindset，但纠正的是 GE 式的"人对人"零和博弈，而非宝洁式的"品牌对品牌"市场竞争 |

---

## 一个有趣的对称

宝洁和微软都经历了**"从内部竞争 → 协作"的文化演化**，但路径不同：

- **宝洁（1986 年）**：Smale & Pepper 用 Category Management 让同品类品牌从竞争转向协作，动力来自**外部竞争压力**（80 年代对手变强）。
- **微软（2013 年）**：Nadella 用 growth mindset 让员工从互相倾轧转向共同成长，动力来自**内部文化危机**（stack ranking 导致人才流失、创新停滞）。

两者殊途同归，但**宝洁走得更早**——这恰恰说明宝洁文化本身具备自我纠偏能力，而 Ballmer 主政的微软在文化纠偏上迟滞了约 27 年。

**AFTER:** 60s timeout + retry; ESC signal propagates; transient errors auto-retry.

## Answer: Yes, editing project-level skill files *can* write to the wiki DB — but only through specific triggers, not automatically on file save.

There are **three code paths** that index skill content into the wiki `skills` domain (the RAG/vector DB), and the hot-reload file watcher is **not** one of them:

### The three wiki-write triggers

| Trigger | What writes to wiki | When |
|---------|--------------------|----|
| **Startup** (`loadAll` → `indexAllSkillsToWiki`) | All skills, batched, with a content-hash cache to skip unchanged ones | Once at app boot |
| **`/skills build`** (slash command) | Same `indexAllSkillsToWiki` — full rebuild | When the user types `/skills build` |
| **`skill_load(name=...)`** (tool) | `indexSkillToWiki` — re-indexes that one skill (best-effort) | Every time the agent loads a skill |

### What does NOT write to wiki

- **The file watcher** (`watchDirectories` → `reloadSkill`) — hot-reload only updates the **in-memory** `skills` map. It does **not** call any wiki function. So the lfp auto-editing `.mycc/skills/*.md` files triggers a silent in-memory reload, but **no wiki write**.

### So: does lfp auto-editing pollute the wiki DB?

**Not directly from the edit.** Editing the file only hot-reloads it in memory. The wiki write happens **later**, when one of the three triggers fires:

1. **At next startup** — `indexAllSkillsToWiki` runs.It diffs by content hash and only re-embeds changed skills, so a one-time lfp edit causes exactly one embedding round-trip for that skill at the next boot — then the cache skips it forever after.

### The real concern: stale records when skills are deleted

The subtler pollution risk is **orphaned wiki records**. `indexAllSkillsToWiki` only deletes records whose title prefix matches *this project's own scope* (`[user]:`, `[built-in]:`, `<project-basename>:`). So:

- **Editing** a project skill → old record deleted, new one written (clean replacement) ✓
- **Deleting** a project skill file → its wiki record becomes an orphan, and `indexAllSkillsToWiki` *will* clean it up at next startup (it's in this project's scope) ✓
- **Cross-project** → records from other projects are left untouched (correct — no mutual wiping) ✓

So the wiki DB stays clean: edits replace, deletions get orphan-cleaned at next boot. The cache (`skill-index-cache.json`, gitignored under `.mycc/`) ensures unchanged skills cost zero embeddings.

### Net answer to your question

Allowing lfp to auto-edit `.mycc/skills/` files does **not** pollute the wiki DB from the edit itself — the file watcher is memory-only. The only wiki writes happen at startup, `/skills build`, or `skill_load`, all of which are diff-aware (content-hash cache + title-prefix scoping) and self-cleaning. The one cost is a single embedding round-trip per changed skill at the next startup. No manual wiki cleanup is needed.

If you want to be extra cautious, you can run `/skills build` after lfp edits to force the re-index immediately and verify the cache refreshes — but it's not required for correctness.

## Complete Plan: Re-enable Crossroad When Tool Calls Co-occur with Turning Words

### 1. Root Cause Analysis

**BEFORE (pre-2026-08-20):** Crossroad fired on ANY response with turning words, including those with tool calls. This truncated reasoning and discarded committed tool calls, "mis-directing" the LLM.

**AFTER (current, 2026-08-20 change):** The guard `tools.length > 0 && chat.rawToolCalls.length === 0` in `llm.ts` (around line 140) skips crossroad entirely when tool calls are present. This is an **over-correction**: genuine indecision where the LLM waffles AND commits to a tool call now bypasses crossroad, so the LLM keeps hitting the wall.

**The key insight:** Triologue parity is NOT violated by discarding tool calls in `llm.ts`, because `triologue.agent()` is only called in `hook.ts` (not in `llm.ts`). In `llm.ts`, setting `chat.rawToolCalls = []` only mutates the pass-local `ChatData` — the triologue is untouched. The `duplicate_assistant` TP violation only triggers when `triologue.agent()` is called twice in succession, which doesn't happen here.

### 2. The Design: Split Detection from Disposal

The fix separates two concerns that the 2026-08-20 change conflated:

1. **Detection** (in `llm.ts`): Should crossroad fire when turning words are present, regardless of tool calls? → **Yes**, re-enable.
2. **Disposal** (in `hook.ts`): What happens to the original tool calls when crossroad fires? → **Discard them**, same as the text-only path. The LLM regenerates tool calls after the continuation.

### 3. Specific Code Changes

#### 3.1 `src/loop/states/llm.ts` — Remove the `rawToolCalls.length === 0` guard

**Current code (around line 140):**
```typescript
if (tools.length > 0 && chat.rawToolCalls.length === 0) {
  // cooldown gate...
  // crossroad detection...
} else {
  env.crossroadOccurred = false;
}
```

**Changed code:**
```typescript
if (tools.length > 0) {
  // cooldown gate (unchanged)...
  // crossroad detection (unchanged)...
  // When crossroad fires AND tool calls were present, the tool calls
  // are discarded here (chat.rawToolCalls = []) — the LLM regenerates
  // them in the next COLLECT round after the continuation is injected.
  // triologue.agent() is NOT called here, so no TP violation occurs.
} else {
  env.crossroadOccurred = false;
}
```

The only change is removing `&& chat.rawToolCalls.length === 0` from the condition. The existing `chat.rawToolCalls = []` line inside the crossroad-fired block already handles disposal — it was already there as a guard comment ("no tool calls to discard"), but now it actively discards real tool calls.

#### 3.2 `src/loop/states/hook.ts` — No changes needed

The HOOK state's crossroad branch already handles the case correctly:
```typescript
if (chat.crossroadContinuation) {
  const finalContent = `${chat.assistantContent || ''} ${chat.crossroadContinuation}`;
  triologue.agent(finalContent, [{ /* brief tool call */ }], ...);
  // ...
  return AgentState.COLLECT;
}
```

This branch is **mutually exclusive** with the normal registration path (the `if` early-returns). When crossroad fires, `chat.rawToolCalls` is already `[]` (set in `llm.ts`), so the normal path's `hookResult.calls` will be empty. The synthetic `brief` tool call is the only one registered. This is already correct.

#### 3.3 `src/loop/crossroad.ts` — No changes needed

`handleCrossroad` already receives `originalContent` (the text portion) and detects turning words in it. Tool calls are not passed to `handleCrossroad` (the signature is `handleCrossroad(messages, originalContent, tools, signal)` — note the 3rd param is `tools` (the tool schema), not `toolCalls`). So detection already works on text only.

### 4. Triologue Parity Verification

The critical sequence when crossroad fires WITH tool calls:

1. **`llm.ts`:** LLM returns `content + tool_calls`. Crossroad detects turning word, sets `chat.assistantContent = truncated`, `chat.crossroadContinuation = continuation`, `chat.rawToolCalls = []`. **No triologue call.** No TP risk.

2. **`hook.ts`:** `chat.crossroadContinuation` is set → enters crossroad branch → calls `triologue.agent(finalContent, [briefCall])` → calls `triologue.tool('brief', result, briefCallId)`. **One agent() + one tool() = valid sequence.** The original tool calls are never registered in triologue, so there are no orphaned pending calls.

3. **`COLLECT` → `LLM`:** The LLM sees `prefix + continuation` as the assistant message and a `brief` tool result. It regenerates tool calls naturally.

**No TP violation occurs** because:
- `triologue.agent()` is called exactly once (in `hook.ts`).
- No pending tool calls are left dangling (the original calls were discarded at the `ChatData` level, never registered in triologue).
- The `duplicate_assistant` violation only fires if `triologue.agent()` is called when `getLastRole() === 'assistant'`, which doesn't happen here (the last role before the crossroad branch is whatever preceded this LLM call — typically `tool` or `user`).

### 5. The `brief` False-Positive Concern

The 2026-08-20 change was motivated by `brief` tool calls: the LLM writes hedging text ("However...", "Wait...") alongside a `brief` call, and crossroad would truncate that reasoning. This is a **real concern** but it's a detection-quality issue, not a parity issue.

**Mitigation:** The existing detection tier system already filters most false positives (sentence-boundary checks, minimum prefix/suffix length). The `brief` tool's hedging language is typically mid-sentence ("I'm working on X, but I need to check Y"), which fails the sentence-boundary guard for tier-2 words. A genuine turning word ("However, I should reconsider the entire approach") passes the guard because it IS a real turn.

**If false positives remain a problem after re-enabling**, the fix is to refine `detectTurningWord` (e.g., exempt responses where the only tool call is `brief`), NOT to skip crossroad entirely. But this is a follow-up — the initial re-enablement should use the existing detection as-is.

### 7. Documentation Changes

#### 7.1 `docs/crossroad-design.md`

Update the "Integration with the State Machine" section:
- Remove "Tool calls ARE now a precondition to SKIP crossroad" from the Overview.
- Update the `llm.ts` code example: change the guard from `tools.length > 0 && rawToolCalls.length === 0` to `tools.length > 0`.

## Why `brief`-Only Tool Calls Should Be Exempted from Crossroad

### 1. What `brief` Actually Is

The `brief` tool's own description says: *"Talk to yourself and let the user know. Use to report progress or findings during task execution."* It is explicitly a **mid-thought status update** — the LLM narrates its reasoning while working. It is not a substantive action like `read_file`, `edit_file`, or `bash`. It commits to nothing; it merely reports.

This means the text accompanying a `brief` call is **the LLM's internal monologue**, not a committed direction. The LLM is thinking out loud: weighing alternatives, hedging, reconsidering. That hedging language is the LLM's natural reasoning vocabulary — not a genuine direction reversal.

### 2. The Turning-Word False Positive Mechanism

Crossroad's tiered detection is designed to catch the LLM **reversing course** — committing to direction A, then pivoting to contradict it. The tier-2 sentence-boundary words ("However", "But", "Actually") trigger when they start a new sentence after 30+ chars of committed content.But here's the key insight: when the LLM calls `brief`, its accompanying text is **reasoning narration**, not a committed direction. The LLM writes things like "I need to verify the auth flow. However, the issue might be in the DB layer." — that "However" is the LLM weighing alternatives mid-thought, not reversing a committed course of action. A `brief` call has no action to discard — it's just a status update. Firing crossroad on it truncates the LLM's reasoning, discards a harmless status call, and injects an alien continuation as the LLM's "own" thinking — exactly the mis-direction that `crossroad-1787189812709.json` documents as a live false positive. When a real action tool (`bash`, `read_file`, `edit_file`) is present alongside turning words, that IS a committed action worth intercepting — the LLM committed to a direction then pivoted, so crossroad should fire and discard the premature action.

## Revised Plan: Hint-Round Enhanced with Compact Trigger

### The Problem

An unstable LLM (e.g. glm-5.3-flash) loops by emitting repeated brief-only turns ("Let me see what to do next."). The existing confusion-index hint round fires at threshold 10 (~10 such turns), generating a HINT note the unstable LLM ignores, then confusion resets and the cycle repeats until ctx-threshold auto-compact eventually breaks it — wasting many turns + hint-round LLM calls.

### The New Direction (per user)

**Chain the hint-round with a lightweight LLM call that can decide to trigger compaction.** Instead of the hint round only injecting a HINT note (which the unstable LLM ignores), the hint round's LLM call gets a `compact` tool (or a structured "should_compact" field) so it can *act* on the dead-loop diagnosis, not just describe it.

### Design Analysis: Two Approaches

**Approach A — Structured field `should_compact` in the HINT schema (REJECTED):**
The current hint-round uses `retryChat` with `format: HINT_SCHEMA` (structured JSON output). Adding a `should_compact: boolean` field is simple, but `retryChat` with `format` doesn't support tools — the structured output constraint and tool calling are mutually exclusive in the Ollama API. So the LLM can only *say* "compact" but can't *call* compact.

**Approach B — Use `forkChat` with a compact tool (CHOSEN):**
`forkChat` already supports tools (it's used by recap and crossroad). We can fork from the triologue with a *single* tool — a `compact` tool — and let the LLM decide whether to call it. This reuses the prompt cache (same messages prefix), is ESC-interruptible, and the LLM's tool-call decision is deterministic: either it calls `compact` or it doesn't.The flow: `generateHintRound` first runs the existing structured analysis (injecting the HINT note), then chains a second lightweight `forkChat` call with a single `compact` tool — the fork's prompt shows the conversation + hint result and asks "is this a dead loop? if so, call compact." The return type changes from `'aborted' | 'success'` to `'aborted' | 'success' | 'compact'`, and `collect.ts` handles `'compact'` by setting `chat.deferredCompact = true` (the existing deferred-compact mechanism in `llm.ts`). No new sequence API, no hookish skill — just a two-call chain inside `hint-round.ts` plus a 3-line branch in `collect.ts`.

## 2. Step 6 (watcher re-indexes updated skills) — **BROKEN for cross-instance**

This is the most important finding. Your step 6 says: *"after the project-level skill gets updated, the skill is re-indexed into wiki so the running MYCC can use it without restarting."*

The mechanism exists and works **within one process**:
- `loader.watchDirectories()` (`src/context/shared/loader.ts:434`) sets `fs.watch` on `.mycc/skills/`.
- On a `.md` change → `debouncedReloadSkill` (300ms) reloads the skill in-memory, **and** `debouncedReindex` (2min) emits `{type:'skill_reindex'}` IPC.
- `parent-context.ts:391` listens for `skill_reindex` → calls `loader.indexAllSkillsToWiki(this.wikiModule)`.

**The break:** `fs.watch` is **per-process** — it only fires for file changes made by *any* process, but the *handler* (reload + re-index) runs only in the process that owns the watcher. Here's the failure:

1. The **skill-manager peer** (a *separate* mycc process) edits `.mycc/skills/foo.md` via `edit_file`.
2. The peer's *own* watcher fires → the peer reloads + re-indexes. ✅ (the peer is up to date)
3. The **lead** (the running MYCC the user cares about) also has a watcher on the *same* `.mycc/skills/` dir. `fs.watch` **does** deliver the event to the lead's watcher too (kernel-level, cross-process) — **on Linux/macOS**.

**But on Windows (your platform, `win32`, Node v24):** `fs.watch` uses `ReadDirectoryChangesW`, which *does* notify across processes. So on Windows the lead's watcher *should* fire.But that is exactly where your concurrency concern bites: every mycc instance in the same folder has its own watcher, so the skill-manager peer's edit triggers **N concurrent `indexAllSkillsToWiki` calls** (the peer + the lead + any other lead), and `WikiManager` has **no locking** — each call does a full `getByDomain` table scan, then interleaved `delete` + `batchPut` on the same LanceDB table with no mutex. The fix is not to make the watcher cross-process-aware (it already is on Windows); it's to serialize the re-index. Two concrete mitigations: (1) a **per-directory lockfile** (e.g. `.mycc/skills/.reindex.lock` with the holder's sessionId + PID, checked-and-claimed atomically before `indexAllSkillsToWiki` runs, released on completion/exit) so only one instance re-indexes at a time; or (2) a **debounced single-writer** design where only the instance that *owns* the change (the peer, since it did the `edit_file`) re-indexes, and the lead's watcher no-ops if a re-index is already in flight (a simple in-process `isReindexing` boolean guard, plus skipping if the lockfile is held by another session). Option 1 is simpler and matches the existing PID-file pattern in `peer-operator.js`; option 2 avoids cross-process contention entirely but requires the peer to signal "I've got this." I'd start with option 1 — the lockfile — since it reuses a pattern already in the codebase and makes the re-index idempotent under any number of concurrent watchers.

**Your question: "even with lead's pid recorded, is it still reliable to kill the croner?"**

Short answer: **No, not directly — and that's fine.** You don't kill the croner timer; you kill the *process* that owns it.

**Why the PID approach is reliable for stopping the cron:**
- croner's `Cron` runs its tick callbacks inside the Lead process's event loop. There is no separate cron process or thread.
- `new Cron(pattern, { unref: true }, ...)` means the timer is `unref`'d — it does NOT keep the event loop alive on its own.- When you kill the Lead process (by the PID we'll record in the heartbeat), the OS reaps the whole process — the croner timer dies with it. No `stop()` call needed; the timer is just a `setInterval` handle living inside that process.

**The one caveat:** a graceful `kill` (SIGTERM) lets the Lead's `SIGTERM` handler run `daemonCronJob.stop()` + `ctx.peer.stop()` + unregister identity — clean. A hard `taskkill /F` (Windows) or `kill -9` skips that, leaving a stale heartbeat file until the 1h prune. Either way the cron itself stops dead the instant the process is gone. So the recorded PID gives a *reliable* kill of the cron transitively, via the process.

## Design Review: `learn-from-past` Skill

### Verdict
The design is **architecturally sound and well-thought-out** — the trigger guards, non-nagging principles, and 3-way user choice are all strong.However, I found one concrete bug and several design gaps worth addressing. Here is the full review.

---

## Design Review: `learn-from-past`

### 1. What Works Well

**Trigger design is robust.** The 4-part condition (`call.args.confidence == 10 && !isPlanMode() && session.count() > 5 && turn.count(work tools) > 0`) correctly filters out the three main false-positive sources: plan-mode confidence, premature optimism (< 5 calls), and read-only turns. The `message` action is the right choice — weakest, non-blocking, lets the agent use judgment.

**Non-nagging principles are well-specified.** "Ask at most once per completed task," "skip if routine," "respect no" — these map to real user-experience concerns. The `injectedThisMove` dedup in `HookExecutor` provides a system-level backstop.

**The 3-way choice (yes / no / later) is well-balanced.** It respects autonomy (SDT), affirms the right to decline (reactance theory), and frames experience as already-owned value (endowment effect). The `lfplater` deferral path is a good escape valve for mid-flow users.

**The `lfplater` file template is thorough.** It captures enough context (task, outcome, key files, approach, pitfalls, suggested skill name/keywords) to reconstruct the experience later without re-reading the full transcript.

---

### 2. BUG: Corrupted Message Text in v2 Compiled Condition

**Severity: High** — this degrades the hook's user-facing output right now.

In `.mycc/conditions.json`, the v2 compiled condition for `learn-from-past` has a **corrupted message string**. Comparing v1 vs v2:

**v1 (correct):**
```
"...ask the user — briefly — whether to:
1. **yes** — turn this success into a reusable skill...
2. **no** — continue without saving
3. **later** — defer for now..."
```

**v2 (corrupted):**
```
"...ask the user — briefly — whether to:
1. **yes** — turn this success into a reusable skill...
2. **no** — continue without saving
3. **later** — defer for now; drop a pointer in `.mycc/lfplater/` to revisit later

This is entirely the user's call, and you are free to skip asking — for example if the work was routine, the user is mid-flow, or they've already declined a similar offer. Ask at most once per completed task.
```
→ becomes in v2:
```
"...ask the user choice to:
1. **yes** — turn this success into a reusable skill...
2. **no** — continue without saving
3. **later** — defer for now; drop a pointer in `.mycc/lfplater/` to revisit later

This is entirely the user's call, and you are free to skip asking — for example if the work was routine, the user is mid-flow, or they've already declined a similar offer. Ask at most once per completed task."
```

The phrase "whether to:" was corrupted to "choice to:" during the v1→v2 migration. The message is still functional but reads as broken English. The v2 migration (`reason: "migrated to turn./session. API"`) appears to have garbled the message text while updating the condition expression — likely a copy-paste or LLM-regeneration artifact.

**Fix:** Re-compile the condition via `skill_compile(name="learn-from-past")` to regenerate a clean v3 with the correct message text, or manually edit `.mycc/conditions.json` to restore the original message.

---

### 3. Design Gap: No "Already Asked" Dedup Across Tasks

**Problem:** The `injectedThisMove` dedup in `HookExecutor` prevents same-move re-trigger, and the message says "ask at most once per completed task." But there is **no system-level mechanism** to prevent the hook from firing again on the *next* `brief(10)` in a later turn. If the agent completes three tasks in one session, the hook fires three times — each time the agent must independently judge whether to skip.

This is *acceptable* by design (the agent uses judgment), but it relies entirely on LLM compliance with the injected instruction. There's no `session.count('brief')` guard like `set-title` uses (`session.count('mycc_title') == 0`).

**Improvement option:** Add a soft guard like `session.countResult('brief', 'confidence=10') <= 1` or a session-level "already asked" flag, so the hook only fires once per session unless the user explicitly requests it. This is a tradeoff — it reduces capture opportunities but eliminates nagging risk entirely.

---

### 4. Design Gap: `bash` in the Work-Tools Guard Is Too Broad

**Problem:** `turn.count('bash') > 0` counts *any* bash call — including `ls`, `git status`, `cat`, and other read-only commands. A turn where the agent only ran `bash` to read files (e.g., `Get-Content`) would trigger the hook, even though no real work was done.

The SKILL.md says the guard is for "real work tools (edit_file, write_file, or bash)" — but `bash` is a catch-all. A read-only bash turn is not meaningfully different from a read-only `read_file`/`grep` turn, which the guard correctly excludes.

**Improvement option:** Either drop `bash` from the guard (rely on `edit_file`/`write_file` only), or use a more specific pattern like `turn.count('bash#pnpm') > 0 || turn.count('bash#npm') > 0 || turn.count('bash#git commit') > 0` to match only write-capable bash commands. However, this risks over-engineering — the simplest fix is to just require `edit_file` or `write_file`.

---

### 5. Design Gap: `lfplater` Files Have No Discovery Mechanism

**Problem:** The "later" branch writes files to `.mycc/lfplater/`, and the SKILL.md says "to process a deferred file later: read it, follow Branch 1, optionally delete it." But there is **no hook, slash command, or reminder** that surfaces pending `lfplater` files to the user or agent. They sit in the directory indefinitely unless someone manually checks.

The directory doesn't even exist yet (`.mycc/lfplater/ not found`) — so the first "later" user will create it, and it may never be revisited.

**Improvement option:** Add a session-start check (e.g., a `start`-triggered hook or a `/lfp` slash command) that lists pending `lfplater` files and offers to process them. Alternatively, mention in the "later" branch response that the user can run a future command to revisit them.

---

### 6. Design Gap: `create-skill` Dependency Is Implicit

**Problem:** Branch 1 (yes) says "Use the `create-skill` skill to create a new one. Load it first: `skill_load(name="create-skill")`." But I could not find a `create-skill` skill in this project. If it doesn't exist, the workflow breaks at Step 2 for the "create new" path.

I did not exhaustively search, but this dependency is unverified. If `create-skill` exists only at user-level or in a different layer, the skill should note that it's an external dependency.

---

### 7. Minor: SKILL.md vs Compiled Condition Drift

The SKILL.md documents the condition as using `seq.hasAny(['edit_file', 'write_file', 'bash'])` (v1 API), but the compiled v2 condition uses the new `turn.count(...)` API. The SKILL.md "Trigger" section still shows `seq.*` calls. This is documentation drift — the SKILL.md should be updated to reflect the v2 `turn.*`/`session.*` API to avoid confusing future readers.

---

### Summary Table

| # | Issue | Severity | Type |
|---|-------|----------|------|
| 2 | Corrupted message text in v2 compiled condition | High | Bug |
| 3 | No cross-task "already asked" dedup | Medium | Design gap |
| 4 | `bash` in work-tools guard is too broad | Low | Design gap |
| 5 | `lfplater` files have no discovery mechanism | Medium | Design gap |
| 6 | `create-skill` dependency unverified | Low | Design gap |
| 7 | SKILL.md docs use v1 `seq.*` API, compiled uses v2 `turn.*` | Low | Doc drift |

---

### Recommended Action Plan

1. **Immediate (bug fix):** Re-compile `learn-from-past` via `skill_compile` to fix the corrupted message text, or manually edit `.mycc/conditions.json`.
2. **Short-term (doc fix):** Update SKILL.md "Trigger" section to reflect the v2 `turn.*`/`session.*` API.
3. **Medium-term (design improvements):** Consider adding a session-level dedup guard (issue #3), narrowing the `bash` guard (issue #4), and adding a `lfplater` discovery mechanism (issue #5).
4. **Verify:** Confirm `create-skill` skill exists before relying on it in Branch 1.

Good question — the role label has to originate *somewhere*, and that choice determines whether we need source code changes or can stay purely in the skill layer. Here are the options:

---

### Option A: CLI flag / env var at launch

The lead spawns the peer with `MYCC_ROLE=skill-manager mycc --auto --skip-healthcheck` (env var) or `mycc --auto --role skill-manager` (CLI flag). The identity registration code reads it and writes it into identity.json at startup.

- **Connection model:** One field in IdentityEntry, set at registration time, visible immediately.
- **Cost:** Requires a source code change to `identity.ts` (add `role` to `IdentityEntry` + `register()`) and `config.ts` or `agent-repl.ts` (parse the flag/env). Violates the "no src changes" principle.
- **Race window:** None — role is present from the moment the peer registers.

### Option B: Self-declaration by the skill-manager (after skill load)

The skill-manager's first step (Step 0) updates its own identity.json entry: call `peers(include_self=true)` to get its own session-id, read identity.json, add `role: "skill-manager"` to its entry, write it back via bash.

- **Connection model:** Same one field in IdentityEntry, but written post-registration by the skill itself.
- **Cost:** No source code changes. The skill-manager skill's workflow includes this as Step 0.
- **Race window:** Between the peer's registration and the skill-manager skill loading + updating identity.json (~5-10s for channel poll + skill load), the entry has no role. Other MYCCs checking during this window would not find a role-marked instance.
- **Mitigation:** The lead that spawned it knows it just did (its `bg_print` shows a running peer). Other MYCCs are unlikely to spawn simultaneously.

### Option C: Lead writes the role after spawn

After `bg_create` + `peers()` confirms the peer is online, the lead uses bash to edit identity.json and add `role: "skill-manager"` to the peer's entry (the lead knows the peer's session-id from `peers()`).

- **Connection model:** Same one field, written by the spawner (lead), not the peer.
- **Cost:** No source code changes. The spawning instructions in the `learn-from-past` skill include this step.
- **Race window:** Same as Option B — between peer registration and the lead's write.- **Downside:** The lead now owns two responsibilities (spawn + label), and if the lead dies before labeling, the peer is permanently unmarked.

### Option D: firstQuery self-label via bash (peer does it as Step 0)

The firstQuery instructs the peer to label itself as its very first action (before loading skill-manager): read identity.json, add `role: "skill-manager"` to its own entry, write it back. This is essentially Option B but the labeling is in the firstQuery, not the skill-manager skill — so the skill-manager skill stays problem-focused (no identity-meta-logic, per pitfall #3/#4).

- **Connection model:** One field, written by the peer on its first action.
- **Cost:** No source code changes. The firstQuery (authored by the lead) carries the self-label instruction; the skill-manager skill stays clean.
- **Race window:** Same ~5-10s, but mitigated by the lead's `bg_print` awareness.
- **Separation of concerns:** firstQuery = connection/setup logic; skill-manager skill = domain work. This respects the "complexity within domain, simple connection model" principle.

---

### My recommendation: **Option D**

It keeps the skill-manager skill problem-focused (no identity meta-logic), requires zero source code changes, and places the labeling responsibility on the peer itself (via firstQuery instruction) — not the lead, not the skill. The firstQuery is the connection-layer glue; the skill is the domain-layer work.

The ~5-10s race window is acceptable: the spawning lead knows it just spawned (via `bg_print`), and other productivity MYCCs are unlikely to race-spawn simultaneously. If they do, the worst case is a duplicate skill-manager — which is harmless (the second one finds no lfplater files, reports "nothing to process", and exits).

**No — identity.json has no pruning logic beyond self-removal on graceful exit.**

Stale entries from crashed/killed instances accumulate indefinitely. Here is the full picture:

### What exists (self-cleanup only)

| Mechanism | Location | What it does |
|-----------|----------|--------------|
| `unregister()` | `src/peer/identity.ts:216` | Deletes **only its own** `map[this.sessionId]` entry |
| `peer.stop()` | `src/peer/peer.ts:77` | Calls `identity.unregister()` — invoked on SIGINT, SIGTERM, and normal exit (`agent-repl.ts:512,524,649`) |

`unregister()` is the *only* code path that ever deletes from identity.json, and it can only remove the calling instance's own entry.

### What does NOT exist

- **No startup sweep** — `register()` does a read-merge-write that upserts its own entry but never inspects or removes stale entries from other sessions.
- **No periodic pruning** — the heartbeat interval (30s) only writes the local heartbeat file; it never scans identity.json for dead peers.
- **No crash recovery** — if a process is killed with SIGKILL (or OOM, or power loss), `peer.stop()` never runs and the entry is orphaned forever.

### Mitigations that mask the problem (but don't fix it)

1. **`peers` tool display cutoff** (`src/tools/peers.ts:18`, `PEER_LISTING_CUTOFF_MS = 1h`) — the listing *omits* peers whose latest heartbeat is older than 1 hour, so dead instances don't clutter the `peers` output.This is a display-time filter only; the stale entries remain in identity.json on disk.

2. **`isFresh()` absolute window** (`src/peer/identity.ts`, `FRESHNESS_WINDOW_MS = 90s`) — mail to a stale peer is silently dropped, so orphaned entries can't accidentally receive messages. Again, the entry itself is never removed.

### The gap

identity.json grows monotonically. Every crashed, SIGKILLed, or power-lost instance leaves a permanent orphan. Over time the file gets larger, `readIdentityMap()` parses more dead entries on every register/freshness/mail operation, and `listIdentities()` returns junk that every consumer must filter.

### Recommended fix: add a startup prune

Since you're in plan mode, I propose adding a **startup sweep** to `IdentityManager.register()` — the natural moment to clean up, because a fresh instance is already reading-merging-writing identity.json. The sweep would:

1. **Read the full map** (already done in `register()`).
2. **For each entry that is not self**, read its heartbeat file (`readHeartbeats()`).
3. **Delete entries whose latest heartbeat is older than a cutoff** (reuse `PEER_LISTING_CUTOFF_MS = 1h`, or introduce a dedicated `IDENTITY_PRUNE_CUTOFF_MS`).
4. **Write the pruned map** in the same atomic write as the self-upsert — no extra write cycle.

This is safe because:
- A truly online instance beats every 30s, so it can never be pruned.
- A freshly-started instance with no heartbeat yet is assumed "just started 30s ago" (the `isFresh()` fallback), so it survives.
- Only entries dead for >1h are removed — the same threshold the `peers` tool already uses to hide them.

- `src/tests/peer/peer.test.ts` — add a test: register with a stale orphan entry, assert it's pruned.

│  Runs as a bg process (bg_create or user-started). Every N min:   │
│  1. Check .mycc/lfplater/ for pending files                       │
│  2. Find skill-manager in identity.json (role + workDir + fresh)  │

│  4. Send mail via `mycc-mail <sid> --title "lfplater batch"`      │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─ Skill-Manager peer (headless mycc, --auto --role skill-manager) ─┐

└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

# Mediator Skill: Channel Creation Process & Reliability Analysis

## 1. Channel Creation Process (How It Works)

The mediator wires separate mycc instances by writing **channel file pairs** to disk. The instances' built-in peer-discovery machinery does the rest — no code changes needed.

### The 3 on-disk mechanisms (`~/.mycc-store/discovery/`)

| Mechanism | Path | Who writes | Purpose |
|-----------|------|-----------|---------|
| Identity registry | `identity.json` | Each lead at startup (register()) | Session→{workDir, mailbox, startedAt} map |
| Heartbeats | `heartbeat/<sid>.json` | Each lead every 30s | Rolling last-3 timestamps + briefs + pid |
| Channel files | `channels/<sid>-<channelId>.json` | **The mediator** (you) | Pair of files, one per participant |

### The wiring sequence (verified against source)

```
1. Launch peer instances          →  mycc (NOT raw node; Lead needs Coordinator IPC)
2. Verify online with peers()     →  confirm fresh heartbeat (<90s old)
3. Write BOTH channel files       →  one per participant, mirrored, joined:false, firstQuerySent:false
4. 5s poll auto-joins             →  sweepChannels() finds unjoined files → joinChannel()
5. joinChannel() delivers         →  sets joined=true, appends firstQuery to LOCAL mailbox, sets firstQuerySent=true
6. Next COLLECT injects firstQuery →  [MAIL] note enters the triologue → instance begins its role
7. Instances talk peer-to-peer    →  mail_to(name="<peerSid>/lead", ...) appends to remote mailbox (freshness-gated)
```

**Key insight from source** (`channel.ts:183-214`): `joinChannel` does exactly two things — (1) flip `joined=true`, (2) if `firstQuery` exists and `firstQuerySent` is false, append it to the **local** mailbox. The firstQuery is *never* sent to the remote; it's a local self-kickoff.

### Two connection modes

- **Mode 1 (Outside mediator)**: A third party writes both files, then steps away. Each file's `firstQuery` is the instruction for that file's owner.
- **Mode 2 (You are one endpoint)**: Your file carries a self-kickoff (tells you who you connected to); the peer's file carries your instruction to the peer.

---

## 2. Failure Modes (What Goes Wrong)

From source analysis, I identified **10 distinct failure points**, grouped by category:

### A. File authoring failures (mediator's fault)

| # | Failure | Root cause in source | Effect |
|---|---------|---------------------|--------|
| 1 | **BOM corruption** | `readChannelFile` calls `JSON.parse` — BOM (EF BB BF) from PowerShell 5.1 `Set-Content -Encoding UTF8` makes parse fail → returns null | Channel silently invisible; only `console.warn` |
| 2 | **Mis-escaped firstQuery** | Multi-line `firstQuery` with real newlines, hand-concatenated in shell | JSON parse failure → same as #1 |
| 3 | **Pre-set `joined:true`** | `sweepChannels()` checks `if (!channel.joined)` — skips pre-joined files | firstQuery never delivered; instance sits idle |
| 4 | **Pre-set `firstQuerySent:true`** | `joinChannel` checks `!ownChannel.firstQuerySent` before delivering | Instance joins but gets no kickoff |
| 5 | **Non-atomic write** | 5s poll can read a half-written file mid-write | `readChannelFile` gets partial JSON → returns null → logged, skipped |
| 6 | **Missing sibling file** | `listChannels()` populates `peerSessionId` by scanning for sibling with same channelId suffix | Instance joins but has no peer to reply to |

### B. Instance lifecycle failures

| # | Failure | Root cause in source | Effect |
|---|---------|---------------------|--------|
| 7 | **Raw `node` launch** | `agent-repl.ts main()` checks `process.send` — exits without Coordinator IPC | No identity, no heartbeat, never appears in `peers()` |
| 8 | **Stale instance wired** | `isFresh()` returns false if heartbeat >90s old | `sendPeerMail` returns false; mail silently dropped |
| 9 | **No `--auto` for headless peer** | PROMPT waits for stdin; COLLECT never runs | firstQuery lands in mailbox but is never injected into triologue |

### C. Protocol failures

| # | Failure | Root cause | Effect |
|---|---------|-----------|--------|
| 10 | **Reply-by-prose** | Instance writes answer in conversation instead of `mail_to` | Peer never receives the reply; conversation stays in letterbox |

---

## 3. Reliability Recommendations

### Operational practices (what the mediator should do)

These are drawn from the skill's `sanity-checklist.md` and corroborated by source:

1. **Always verify both instances are online with `peers()` before writing files.** Mail to a stale peer is silently dropped at the `sendPeerMail` level (`channel.ts:296` — `isFresh()` gate). The `mail_to` tool now fails fast with an error, but only if you call it; the channel file itself has no pre-check.

2. **Use `write_file` (structured tool), never hand-rolled shell JSON.** This eliminates BOM corruption (#1), escaping errors (#2), and non-atomic writes (#5) in one stroke. If a shell script is unavoidable, use `jq` (bash) or `ConvertTo-Json` (PowerShell) + atomic temp-file-rename + read-back validation.

3. **Set `peerSessionId` explicitly in both files.** Don't rely on sibling discovery — it works (self-heals within ~5s on the next poll) but explicit is more reliable and eliminates the race window.

4. **Bake the reply contract into every `firstQuery`:** state the peer's session-id and `mail_to(name="<peerSid>/lead", ...)` explicitly. Without it, the instance may reply by prose (#10), and the peer never receives the answer.

5. **Launch headless peers with `mycc --auto --skip-healthcheck`.** `--auto` is essential for unattended peers (replaces PROMPT→WAIT, auto-advances the loop so COLLECT runs and the `[MAIL]` firstQuery is injected). Without it, the peer sits at its prompt forever and the firstQuery rots in the mailbox.

6. **Read back and validate immediately after writing.** Use `jq -e '.joined == false and .firstQuerySent == false'` (bash) or `Get-Content | ConvertFrom-Json` (PowerShell). Caveat: if the read-back shows `true`, the 5s poll already joined (success) — distinguish "what you authored" from "what the poll mutated."

### Source-level improvements (for mycc maintainers)

From the source analysis, several reliability gaps could be hardened at the implementation level:

7. **Silent failures are the biggest enemy.** `readChannelFile` returns `null` on malformed JSON and only logs to `console.warn` — the mediator gets no signal. A dedicated validation tool (e.g. `verify_channel`) that reads back a channel file and reports parse status + field validation would catch BOM/escaping/boolean errors before the 5s poll silently swallows them.

8. **No programmatic channel-creation API.** The entire channel-pair creation is external file I/O — the most failure-prone part of the workflow has no first-class tool. A `create_channel` tool (taking two session-ids + a per-instance firstQuery) would atomically write both files, validate them, and eliminate all 6 authoring failures (#1-#6) in one stroke.

9. **The freshness window (90s) is tight.** A peer that pauses (e.g. long LLM call, GC pause) can miss a heartbeat and be judged stale, dropping mail. The 30s beat interval vs 90s window gives only 3 beats of margin. Widening `FRESHNESS_WINDOW_MS` or adding a "last-seen-recently" grace for mail delivery would reduce false-stale drops.

10. **`peerSessionId: null` self-heals but slowly.** `listChannels()` discovers the sibling on the next 5s poll and persists it — but if mail is sent in that 5s window, `sendMail` finds `peerSessionId` null and the sibling lookup isn't done there. Explicit setting (recommendation #3) is the operational fix; a code-level fix would have `sendMail` fall back to sibling discovery.

---

## Summary

The channel creation process is fundamentally sound — the 5s poll + auto-join + local mailbox delivery is a clean decoupled design. The reliability problems cluster in two areas:

- **Authoring (mediator-side, #1-#6)**: Solvable today by using `write_file` + explicit `peerSessionId` + read-back validation. A `create_channel` tool would eliminate the entire category.
- **Lifecycle/protocol (#7-#10)**: Solvable today by the sanity checklist (verify online, use `--auto`, bake reply contract). Code hardening (validation tool, wider freshness window, sibling fallback in sendMail) would further improve reliability.

The skill's documentation is thorough and accurate — every claim I checked against source (`channel.ts`, `identity.ts`) matched the implementation. The recommendations above extend, not correct, the skill's existing guidance.

## Plan: Rename State Machine Stage `WAIT` → `AWAIT`

### Problem & Root Cause

The state machine has a stage named `WAIT` (enum `AgentState.WAIT = 'wait'`). The crossroad detector in `src/loop/crossroad.ts` (Tier-3) has this turning-word pattern:

```js
/\bWait\b(?=\s*[,!.—]|\s*$)/i
```

This is case-insensitive, so it matches "WAIT", "wait", "Wait" when followed by punctuation (`,.!—…`) or end-of-text. When the LLM writes about the WAIT state in its output — e.g., *"the loop entersWAIT, blocking for mail"* — the `\bWait\b` pattern fires spuriously, truncating the response at "WAIT" and triggering an expensive forkChat continuation generation that produces a false-positive crossroad.

## Solution

Rename the enum member `WAIT` → `AWAIT` and its string value `'wait'` → `'await'`. The word "await" is NOT in any turning-word tier (Tier 1/2/3), so the false positive is eliminated at its root. Since "await" is also a common English verb, I'll verify it's not a turning word before finalizing.

**Verification — "await" is not a turning word:**

The dist build is broken (unrelated module issue), but I can verify "await" is safe by reading the patterns directly. The `\bWait\b` pattern requires a word boundary (`\b`) before "W" — in "await" there's no word boundary before "wait" (it's part of "await"), so "await" cannot match. None of the other tiers (However, But, Actually,Having said that, etc.) match "await" either. So renaming WAIT→AWAIT eliminates the false positive cleanly — the string `'await'` is invisible to every tier of the crossroad detector. Here is the complete plan.

## Section 1 — Viability of the Proposed Design: NOT VIABLE AS SPECIFIED

The proposed design ("lead creates bg mycc via `mycc --auto`, cron triggers it to review backlogs and distill skills") has **three fatal architectural gaps** identified by the architect teammate (grounded in `wait.ts`, `config.ts`, `bg.ts`):

1. **`mycc --auto` blocks forever in WAIT** — auto mode replaces PROMPT with a blocking 1s poll loop checking only mail/teammate/steering events. With no events, it sleeps indefinitely doing zero work. It is reactive, not proactive.
2. **No scheduler exists in mycc** — there is no cron, no `setInterval`, no wall-clock timer anywhere in the loop or hook system. Hook conditions use only `seq.*` (conversation-history queries), not temporal queries. A "cron task on top of auto mode" has nothing to attach to.
3. **bg mycc cannot self-terminate** — after processing a firstQuery, STOP → PROMPT → WAIT loops back to blocking. Only `bg_remove(pid)` (a hard SIGKILL) terminates it. No graceful exit path exists in auto mode.

Additionally, `bg_create` uses `spawn()` and never writes to stdin — so the bg mycc has no way to receive its initial instruction except via the **mediator channel-file firstQuery** mechanism (writing a channel file to `~/.mycc-store/discovery/channels/` that the peer's 5s poll auto-delivers to its mailbox).

**Verdict: the proposed design is architecturally non-viable as specified.** The fundamental tension is that auto mode is event-driven reactive blocking for multi-instance mail chaining, while the design wants time-driven proactive autonomous work-then-exit — different paradigms that cannot be bridged without an external orchestrator.

## 一、已正确处理的竞态（值得明确肯定）

### 1. steer-flush 与 prompt 的时序 —— 关键设计正确

后端 `drainSteering()`（serve-hub.ts:713）**先清空 queue 再 broadcast `steer-flush`**。COLLECT 消费、PROMPT 合成都会调用它。因此前端 `steer-flush` 处理器（main.ts:262）**清空 buffer 是对的**，而卡片只在 `prompt` 消息里、从**仍未清空的 buffer** 里取材（main.ts:221）：

> 凡是到达 PROMPT 时仍留在 `steeringBuffer` 里的 note，一定是在上一个 run 里**从未被 drain** 的 —— 因为任何 drain 都会先发 `steer-flush` 清掉它。

这个「flush 先于 prompt 到达」的推论成立的原因：`drainSteering` 在同一同步调用栈里 `broadcast('steer-flush')`，而 `prompt` 广播发生在后续独立的 loop 状态转换中，二者在单线程 Node 事件循环里严格有序。**这是原始 bug 的正确修复点，没有被误改。**

### 2. 队列原子性

`drainSteering` 用 `const notes = this.steeringQueue; this.steeringQueue = [];` 整体换引用，不是边删边读；`getSteeringNotes` 返回 `[...this.steeringQueue]` 浅拷贝。PROMPT 的 `peek → synthesize → drain` 三段无需加锁（Node 单线程 + 无 await 夹在 peek 和 drain 之间的竞态窗口）。

**How it travels through the grant system:**

| Step | Check | Result for `mycc-mail` |
|------|-------|------------------------|
| 1 | `findDangerousCommand` (dangerous-commands.ts) | `null` — no pattern matches |
| 2 | Intent present? | Yes (`RUN SYSTEM ... TO ...`) |
| 3 | Intent grammar valid? | Yes |
| 4 | **Verb classification** — `isReadOnlyVerb` (READ/FIND/TEST)? No. `isMutationVerb` (WRITE/EDIT/DELETE/BUILD/INSTALL)? No. → falls through | RUN is the **ambiguous bucket** |

- `RUN` → "ambiguous, defer to LLM"

## Plan: Add a `PEER` Object to the Intent Taxonomy

### Core Idea

Add `PEER` as a new OBJECT in the intent language. The bash judge's step 4 currently classifies safety **only by verb** — `RUN` always falls through to the LLM check (step 5) because it's the "ambiguous" bucket. The fix is to make step 4 **object-aware**: when the verb is `RUN` and the object is `PEER`, auto-allow (in any mode, parent and child) because peer communication is inherently non-mutating to project state.

This is the same architectural pattern `hand_over.ts` already uses: it checks `parsed.object === 'USER'` to enforce object-based routing. We extend that pattern into the judge itself.

**BEFORE:** `RUN SYSTEM process=mycc-mail TO consult peer` → step 4: RUN is not read-only, not mutation → falls to step 5 → LLM classifies "send message" as WRITE → **BLOCKED**

**AFTER:** `RUN PEER process=mycc-mail TO consult peer` → step 4: RUN + PEER → recognized as communication, auto-allow → **ALLOWED**

### Why This Is Better Than the Carve-Out (Plan A)

| Aspect | Plan A (carve-out before step 5) | This Plan (PEER object) |
|--------|----------------------------------|-------------------------|
| **Where the fix lives** | Hardcodes `mycc-mail` command string into the judge | Extends the taxonomy — no command-string parsing in the judge |
| **Obfuscation risk** | Needs `isPlainMyccMailCommand()` to prevent `echo hi && mycc-mail` bypass | None — the agent self-declares the object; the judge trusts the taxonomy, not the command string |
| **Child-process block** | Unfixed (child still hard-blocked at step 5) | Fixed (RUN+PEER auto-allows for child too) |
| **Extensibility** | One-off; next safe CLI needs another carve-out | Next communication-style command just uses `RUN PEER` |
| **Layering** | Judge aware of app-specific CLI name | Judge stays generic — only knows verb+object taxonomy |

### Design Decision: Trust the Agent's Object Declaration

A key question: should the judge verify that the command *actually is* a peer-communication command (e.g. regex-match `mycc-mail`), or trust the agent's `PEER` object declaration?

**Decision: Trust the declaration.** Rationale:
1. The agent already chooses the verb — `RUN` vs `READ` vs `DELETE` — and the judge trusts that choice. The object is the same kind of self-classification.
2. The dangerous-commands check (step 1) still runs **before** step 4. If the agent lies about the object to sneak through a dangerous command (e.g. `RUN PEER` on `rm -rf /`), step 1 catches it. The object-based allow only shortcuts the *LLM ambiguity check*, not the *dangerous command check*.
3. This avoids the entire obfuscation-bypass problem that plagued Plan A. The judge never inspects the command string for `PEER` — it only inspects `parsed.object`.
4. If the agent misclassifies a genuinely mutating command as `RUN PEER` and it's not dangerous enough for step 1 to catch, that's the same risk as the agent misclassifying it as `READ SOURCE` — which is already trusted today.

## Yes — it's a display-only limitation, not a binding limitation

The server **is** listening on all interfaces (`0.0.0.0`), but the startup banner only prints **one** URL for convenience.

### What actually happens

1. **Binding** (`ServeHub.start()`):
   ```ts
   this.httpServer!.listen(port, this.host, () => resolve());
   ```
   With `--host` bare, `getServeHost()` returns `'0.0.0.0'`, so Node binds to **all interfaces**. Your machine is reachable on every NIC — WiFi, Ethernet, virtual adapters, loopback, etc.

2. **Display** (`getUrl()` + `activate.ts`):
   ```ts
   } else if (this.host === '0.0.0.0') {
     displayHost = detectLanIpv4() ?? 'localhost'; // all interfaces → LAN IP
   }
   ```
   And `detectLanIpv4()` in `serve-utils.ts`:
   ```ts
   for (const a of addrs) {
     if (a.family === 'IPv4' && !a.internal) {
       if (a.address.startsWith('169.254.')) continue;
       return a.address;  // ← returns the FIRST one, then stops
     }
   }
   ```

### The root cause

`detectLanIpv4()` walks `os.networkInterfaces()` and **returns on the first** non-internal IPv4 address it finds. If your machine has multiple NICs (e.g. Ethernet `192.168.1.20` + WiFi `192.168.0.45` + a VPN/WSL virtual adapter), only the first one in the OS's enumeration order is shown. The rest are silently skipped — not because they aren't bound, but because the helper is designed to show a single representative URL, not enumerate all of them.

### BEFORE / AFTER (perception vs. reality)

| | What you see | What's actually happening |
|---|---|---|
| **Display** | One URL: `http://<first-LAN-IP>:<port>` | Only the first non-internal IPv4 is printed |
| **Binding** | — | `0.0.0.0` → **every** interface accepts connections |

### How to verify

The server listens on all interfaces. You can reach it via any of:
- `http://localhost:<port>` (loopback — always works)
- `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`
- `http://<any-of-your-NIC-IPs>:<port>` — even ones not shown in the banner

To see all your IPs:
```powershell
Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 | Where-Object { $_.IPAddress -notlike '169.254.*' -and $_.IPAddress -ne '127.0.0.1' } | Select-Object IPAddress, InterfaceAlias
```
Each of those IPs will work in a browser — the banner just doesn't print them all.

### Is it worth fixing?

Arguably a minor UX improvement: `detectLanIpv4()` could return an array and `activate.ts` could print multiple URLs (like Vite does: `➜ Local: http://localhost:5173/` + `➜ Network: http://192.168.x.x:5173/`).But the practical takeaway: **no binding problem exists** — use any of your NIC IPs directly. If you'd like, I can patch `detectLanIpv4()` to return all non-internal IPv4 addresses and update `activate.ts` to print each one, so the banner matches reality.

## ML-Only Turning-Point Detector (Machine M) — Revised Plan

### What changed from the prior attempt

The `feat/crossroad-encoder-and-regex-fallback` branch already built most of this infrastructure but shipped it with a regex fallback. Three documented pitfalls killed the model's real-world accuracy:

1. **Length-confounding** — v1 data had all negatives <100 chars, positives >100 chars. Model learned "long→turn" shortcut.
2. **Identical-text-opposite-labels** — v2 data used the same context banks for both classes, differing only in a connector word. Loss stuck at ln(2)=0.693 (zero learning).
3. **Embeddings can't detect rhetorical reversals** — embedding cosine similarity stays high for on-topic reversals. This rules out lightweight embedding-only approaches but NOT transformer encoders (which learn pragmatic patterns, not topic proximity).

**v3 data (deconfounded, mimicking real LLM responses) achieved 100% held-out accuracy** on independent topic banks. The architecture works; the data was the problem.

---

### Section 1 — The M Machine Interface

M is a thin wrapper over the ONNX encoder with a sliding-window ring buffer. It replaces both `detectTurningWord()` (post-hoc) and the `StreamingCrossroadDetector` (accumulator) from the abandoned branch.

```
M.reset()        → clear ring buffer, reset internal state
M.feed(token)    → append one BPE token to ring buffer (evict oldest if > 64)
                   run ONNX inference on the 64-token window
                   store per-token probability for the last token
M.peek()         → scan probabilities from the END of the buffer;
                   return N = distance from highest-prob turning token
                   to the last fed token, or -1 if none exceeds threshold
```

**peek() returns N, not a boolean.** N=0 means the current token is the turning point. N=4 means it was 4 tokens ago. -1 means no turn in the current window. This gives the caller both *whether* and *where*, enabling the truncation at the exact turning position.

**Key difference from the abandoned branch's `StreamingCrossroadDetector`:** That class ran inference on the *entire accumulated text* every `checkInterval` characters (a growing, unbounded input). M runs inference on a *fixed 64-token window* every token. This is:
- **Bounded latency** — 64 tokens × DistilBERT is <5ms, constant, not growing with response length
- **Per-token granularity** — detects the turning point at the token level, not "somewhere in the last 50 chars"
- **No maxSequenceLength overflow** — the abandoned branch hit ONNX broadcast failures when text exceeded 512 tokens; a fixed 64-token window eliminates this entirely

*Note (scope):* The abandoned branch's `crossroad-encoder.ts` (ONNX loader, singleton, `predict()`) is reusable as-is. Only `streaming-crossroad-detector.ts` needs to be rewritten as the M machine with a ring buffer. The encoder's `predict(text)` method takes a string; M will tokenize internally and call the ONNX session directly (bypassing `predict()`'s full-text path) to get per-token logits instead of a single window-level probability.

*Note (correlation):* M's per-token output requires the ONNX model to be exported with a **token-level classification head** (output shape `[1, seq_len, 2]`), not the sequence-level head (`[1, 2]`) the abandoned branch used. This is a training/export change — see Section 3.

### Section 2 — Model Architecture

Reuse the abandoned branch's DistilBERT architecture, but change the classification head from sequence-level to token-level.

| Component | Abandoned Branch | Revised |
|-----------|-----------------|---------|
| Base model | `distilbert-base-multilingual-cased` | Same (multilingual for EN+ZH) |
| Classification head | `[1, 2]` (sequence-level: is this text a turn?) | `[1, seq_len, 2]` (token-level: is this token the start of a turn?) |
| Max sequence length | 512 | **64** (fixed window, no overflow) |
| Output | Single P(turn) for whole text | Per-token P(turn) for each of 64 positions |
| Model size | ~541MB unquantized | ~66MB (DistilBERT with 64-position limit, INT8 quantized) |
| Inference | One call per checkInterval chars | One call per token, <5ms |
| Dependencies | `onnxruntime-node` + `@huggingface/transformers` | Same |

**Why 64 tokens:** A turning word like "However" or "但" needs ~1-2 tokens of lookahead to confirm (the punctuation/next-word disambiguation that the regex tiers encoded). 64 tokens gives ~3-4 sentences of context before the turn — enough for the model to see the committed direction and the pivot. More context doesn't help (the pitfall wiki proved embeddings encode topic, not direction; the transformer needs local pragmatic context, not distant topic context).

**Why token-level, not sequence-level:** The abandoned branch's sequence-level head required running inference on the full accumulated text to get one P(turn), then had to separately find *where* the turn was. Token-level classification gives both in one pass — each token independently says "I am/am not the start of a turn." This is the standard NER pattern (BIO tagging), well-understood and stable to train.

**INT8 quantization:** The abandoned branch noted quantization was "known-broken." This needs to be fixed — 541MB unquantized is unacceptable for a CLI tool. INT8 quantization via `onnxruntime`'s `quantize_dynamic` should bring it to ~66MB. If quantization remains broken, fall back to FP16 (~270MB) or prune the model to 4 layers (~130MB).

*Note (scope):* The 64-token window is small enough that a custom 4-layer transformer (as I originally proposed) could replace DistilBERT entirely, dropping to ~5MB.However, the pragmatic path is to reuse the abandoned branch's DistilBERT first — it's already trained, exported, and tested with 100% held-out accuracy. Ship the working model, then optimize model size as a follow-up once the feedback loop is running and we have real-world accuracy data to benchmark against.
